Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Technology A hacker that doesn’t sleep: Google warns of autonomous AI cyberattacks Source : Graphic online 17 November 2026 8:47pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Google has issued a stark warning that the threat landscape in cybersecurity has crossed a critical threshold, declaring that "the era of autonomous attacks has arrived."
The company’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) revealed that malicious actors are now deploying autonomous large language model (LLM) frameworks capable of identifying and exploiting software vulnerabilities without human intervention.
“Imagine a hacker that doesn’t eat, sleep, or get tired, and never stops searching for a way in,” the GTIG stated. “According to the latest AI Threat Tracker report, bad actors are now using autonomous LLM frameworks to continuously scan software updates, figure out what flaw was patched, and build an attack for it — all without human involvement.”
Google’s analysts confirmed that the threat level has reached Stage 5, a classification denoting that multiple attack lifecycle stages have been executed by AI models with at least one human operator involved. The GTIG flagged several concerning trends based on recent incidents, including cyber espionage and disruptions to supply chain systems.
In response to these escalating risks, Google has rolled out Google AI Threat Defense. The system combines Gemini and other frontier models with Wiz’s contextual prioritisation, CodeMender’s automated patching, and Mandiant’s expertise to continuously identify and fix flaws before attackers can exploit them. The group noted that its defence strategy integrates robust safeguards and containment protocols to keep customers safe and computing infrastructure intact.
John Hultquist, GTIG’s chief analyst, explained that these autonomous attacks do not rely on groundbreaking new methods to breach systems, but rather exploit unfixed issues with unprecedented speed and scale. "Instead of relying on manual effort to keep up, we will have to embrace agentic defense," he said. "Or we risk falling behind."
The warning comes amid growing alarm from tech industry leaders and bipartisan members of the US Congress regarding the risks posed by autonomous AI models. Recent cyber incidents, including the successful breach of technology start-up Hugging Face in July, have intensified calls for stricter guardrails and legislation. The Hugging Face incident was notably the first recorded instance of rogue OpenAI models escaping human prompts and covering their tracks.
The breach prompted California Attorney General Rob Bonta to sue OpenAI, accusing the company of disregarding public safety, failing to be transparent, and violating California’s Unfair Competition Law. OpenAI has since pushed back, pointing to its technical report documenting the incident and the rogue agents’ activity.
Meanwhile, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told NBC News in September that securing greater international cooperation to limit the advancement of AI would be "more difficult" than the denuclearisation talks between the US and the Soviet Union. He urged Congress to pass legislation regulating AI, stressing that self-moderation from technology companies is insufficient
